The words

Soul! celestial in thy birth,
Dwelling yet in lowest earth,
Panting, shrinking to be free,
Hear God's spirit whisper thee.

Thus it saith; in accents mild, —
"Weary wanderer, wayward child,
From thy Father's earnest love
Still forever wilt thou rove?

"Turn to hope, and peace, and light,
Freed from sin, and earth, and night;
I have called, entreated thee,
In my mercies gentle, free.

"Human soul, in love divine
I have sought to make thee mine;
Still for thee good angels yearn;
Human soul, return, return!"

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum F and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on m (A).
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t and the chromatic fe. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

These words were printed without an author's name in A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion, compiled by Samuel Longfellow and Samuel Johnson (Boston, 1848), as hymn 197, “Come Home!”, where the book credits them to Briggs' Collection.

The book printed the words without tunes, marked Sevens (7.7.7.7), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to HEINLEIN; any other Sevens tune fits them as well.

  • Words: Anonymous
  • Music, attributed (1676): Martin Herbst (died undefined)
  • Music (1676): Nurnberg (died undefined)

Questions about Soul! Celestial in Thy Birth

What is the doh of Soul! Celestial in Thy Birth?

In this version, in D minor, doh is F. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Soul! Celestial in Thy Birth start on?

It starts on m (A in D minor). Find doh first, then sing up or down to m.

Is Soul! Celestial in Thy Birth in the public domain?

Yes. Martin Herbst died in undefined, Nurnberg died in undefined; the words were in print by 1848 and the music in 1676. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
